# Versioning

How this project versions its commits and the running artifact. The scheme, meaning the manifest's
suffix spelling and the unique-per-commit aim, is generic and shared across projects: this file is
copied **verbatim**, with
[Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) covering each medium by
conditional rather than per-project edits.

## Terms

Three names, used as defined here across
[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md),
[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md), and the notes files:

- **version**: the per-commit version (e.g. `0.3.0-5.3.0`). It lives in the manifest and
  nowhere else. No ladder, chores section, todo entry, commit title, or commit body writes one
  (see
  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](../agent-data/prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)),
  and its suffix encodes the cycle phase for whoever inspects the manifest (see
  [Suffix scheme](#suffix-scheme)).
- **version-of-record**: the authoritative stored copy of the version, in the project's manifest
  (see [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)); a built or running
  artifact derives from it.
- **versioning**: the topic, this scheme as a whole.

## A stamp, not a name

The version answers "which commit produced this artifact". It is not a name for a step: a step is
named by its title and located by its position in the ladder list (see
[Steps are named, not numbered](../agent-data/prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). So the
suffix below is the only number in the system, and since nothing dereferences it, reordering or
inserting a step leaves the versions already committed alone.

## Recording the version-of-record

Where the version-of-record lives, how it's stored and
surfaced, and how often it changes — pick the case that fits
your medium:

- **Manifest** — where the version-of-record is stored:
  - if Rust, `Cargo.toml` `[package].version`
  - if Python, `pyproject.toml` `[project].version` (or the
    committed config it's sourced from)
  - otherwise wherever the medium records it (a generic
    `version.toml`, a book's frontmatter, …) — add the case as
    needed
- **Notation** — how the `-` form is stored:
  - if the format allows `-` (TOML `version.toml`, `Cargo.toml`),
    store it verbatim
  - if it bars `-` (PEP 440's local segment, e.g. a Python
    project), remap to `+` — `0.3.0-5.3.0` → `0.3.0+5.3.0`: same
    version, just the stored spelling
- **Reporter** — how a built artifact surfaces the
  version-of-record:
  - if a CLI app, `<cli-app> -V`
  - if a TUI/GUI, add to Help/About or display on the title
- **Cadence** — how often to bump: see
  [Unique per commit](#unique-per-commit-preference-not-requirement);
  this project follows the per-commit preference.

## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)

Our general notion is that the version-of-record should change
on **every commit**, so a built or running artifact identifies
the exact commit it came from.

- This is a preference, **not** a hard requirement. A project
  following the cycle protocol may bump less often — once per
  cycle, only at release, and so on. Record the choice in
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)
  if it differs.
- It is achievable because the cycle's versions (below) are
  **pre-assignable**, unlike the git SHA, which a commit cannot
  contain (see the cycle protocol's
  [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill)).

## Suffix scheme

The cycle (Preparation -> Work -> Close-out; see [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md)) encodes
each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a Preparation**.

This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is
not a name for a step and it is not written anywhere else: a step is identified by its title, and
a ladder rung carries neither a number nor a version (see
[Steps are named, not numbered](../agent-data/prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). The
identifiers below therefore count commits within a phase; nothing dereferences one.

- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: Work commits
- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)

**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle — no ladder,
no setup commit — skips `-0` and starts at `-1` (its first
Work commit). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle
needing no Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that
grows a Preparation later adds the `0` step without
renumbering siblings.

Disambiguation:

- `-10` — Work commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a
  Preparation.
- `-1.0` — Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final
  identifier `0`).

**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:

- `X.Y.Z-3.0` — Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2` — its Work
- `X.Y.Z-3` — its Close-out
- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0` — Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle

Bump the version-of-record at the start of each phase, so the
active phase is recorded — and, per the preference above,
every commit carries a distinct version.

## Suffix scheme

The cycle (Preparation -> Work -> Close-out; see [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md)) encodes
each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a Preparation**.

This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is
not a name for a step and it is not written anywhere else: a step is identified by its title, and

identifiers below therefore count commits within a phase; nothing dereferences one.

- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: Work commits
- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)

**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle — no ladder,
no setup commit — skips `-0` and starts at `-1` (its first
Work commit). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle
needing no Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that
grows a Preparation later adds the `0` step without
renumbering siblings.

Disambiguation:

- `-10` — Work commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a
  Preparation.
- `-1.0` — Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final
  identifier `0`).

**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:

- `X.Y.Z-3.0` — Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2` — its Work
- `X.Y.Z-3` — its Close-out
- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0` — Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle

Bump the version-of-record at the start of each phase, so the
active phase is recorded — and, per the preference above,
every commit carries a distinct version.

content.text:
`notes/versioning.md` is clean: 0 banned characters, and the one over-width line is the unwrappable link.

**On your questions**

Your Done-entry model is already the rule, so nothing needs changing there. One entry per cycle, its `[[N]]` landing on the chores `##` header with the as-built ladder as the first content under it. Single-commit cycles are just one-rung ladders, so the shape doesn't special-case.

The ancestry premise was the one thing off: all eight dynamic-warmup commits **are** ancestors of `main` (the trapezoid rewrite landed them; the `dynamic-warmup` bookmark is gone), so those versions and SHAs are final and the rungs are backfillable now. The genuinely-will-change case is 0.24.1 on the unlanded `agent-files-model`.

And I'd revise my "same beat as the SHA" line from last turn: your pasted ladders write the version at rung-open, which is right, because the version is known then and the SHA isn't. They share only the correction beat. So both ladders you pasted are already in target form.

**What's left, as one batch when you want it**

1. One correction first, because it changes what happens: **`feat: dynamic warmup` is not on `measure-reproducibility`.** It landed on `main` (all eight rungs are ancestors of `main` via the trapezoid rewrite; the `dynamic-warmup` bookmark is deleted). What's actually sitting on `measure-reproducibility` is a different, in-flight cycle of three commits: `feat: measure reproducibility opening`, `feat: report the power policy and clock quantum`, `refactor: extract the report renderer`. So the rebase moves *that* ladder, not dynamic warmup's.

**Your rule is right, and better than the walk-back I made last turn.** I said the version should go in at rung-open because it is knowable then. You're pointing out that knowable is not the same as trustworthy: on an unlanded branch a version is exactly as unstable as a SHA, so it should inherit the SHA's timing rather than get its own. That gives one rule at one beat instead of two rules at two beats, and `notes.md`'s Timing section already states it for SHAs ("on a topic branch a section waits until the branch lands"). The version just joins that sentence.

The trade, stated rather than glossed: we give up recording a fact we could have recorded earlier. `versioning.md` even points out the version is "pre-assignable, unlike the git SHA". We pay that to get a record that a rebase cannot falsify.

**And that is the payoff in front of us: it makes the rebase free in the records.** Nothing renumbers, because nothing is numbered. No version is written yet, because nothing has landed. So rebasing `measure-reproducibility` onto `agent-files-model` touches its ladder not at all: same titles, same order, same bare rungs. The only thing the rebase moves is `Cargo.toml` content inside each commit, which no longer appears in prose. Compare that to the old form, where the same rebase would have invalidated a version in every rung.

**Concretely, for the three ladders in play:**

- **`## feat: dynamic warmup`**: landed, so both facts are writable now. Backfill the eight refs and keep the versions, which are final. This is the one that needs work, and it needs no renumbering.
- **`## docs: experiment in the local agent-files`**: unlanded on this bookmark, so under your rule its `0.24.1` comes *out* and the rung waits as a bare title. Same for this step's own rung, which is already bare.
- **`measure-reproducibility`'s section**: bare titles until the branch lands, which is what the rule produces by default.

**One expectation to reset:** you're anticipating a renumber, and I don't think there is one. `agent-files-model`'s tip is 0.24.2, so the branch's `0.25.0-0/-1/-2` remain valid and monotonic after the rebase. A renumber would only be needed if we insert or reorder steps, and even then it happens in `Cargo.toml` alone.

**The plain version:** dynamic warmup already landed on main, so it is the ladder to backfill, not the one to rebase; the branch holds the three measure-reproducibility commits. Your rule is the better one and I'd take it over what I said last turn: a version goes into the record at the same moment a SHA does, never before landing. The reward is exactly the case you're about to run, since the rebase then costs nothing in the notes, and the price is that we hold back a fact we could have written early.

No version appears in durable prose: not in a ladder rung, a chores header or as-built ladder, a
`## Done` entry, `done.md`, a commit title, or a commit body. The manifest is the version's only
written home (see [versioning.md](../notes/versioning.md)), and a commit's version is read from
that file at that commit.

**Why:** the version is a build stamp answering "which commit produced this artifact", not a name
for a step. Written into prose it becomes a second identifier that history is free to invalidate:
one renumber of published versions turns every prose mention, transcript and pasted report into
residue that needs a decoder to read. A renumber cannot touch a title.

**How to apply:** name the step by its title and the phase in words ("the close-out", "the
opening"). Existing versioned prose is grandfathered and converts when touched, no sweep.

### Commits backfill

An as-built ladder rung cites its commit by SHA, but a SHA
isn't stable until the commit lands on a **permanent
branch** (`main`, or a long-lived release/patch branch that
won't be rewritten); a rebase or squash rewrites it on the
way. So:

- A rung is **written with the literal `[[N]]`
  placeholder**.
- **Backfill once the commit is on a permanent branch**,
  where its SHA is final. A commit can't record its own SHA
  (that would change the hash), so the fill always lands one
  push later: **each push backfills the rungs of the
  commits the previous push made permanent.** On a topic
  branch the sections instead wait until the branch lands,
  so no SHA is ever written that a later rebase could
  invalidate.

Backfill replaces the placeholder with a file-local `[[N]]`
ref, defined as the commit URL + 40-hex SHA in the file's
`# References` (format in agent-data/notes.md
[Chores commit references](../agent-data/notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
Sections predating the ladder form keep their legacy
`Commits:` lines; backfill those where they exist. A
section's `##` title matches its commit title, so a rare
deliberate rewrite of a permanent-branch commit re-syncs via
`git log --grep "<title>"`.

The per-push cadence is a project choice, not dogma: a
**per-close-out** model (recording a cycle's SHAs at its
close-out) is equally valid. The one invariant: a recorded
SHA must be permanent.

## Per-commit checklist

Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out), per the protocol's
[Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow):

1. Mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
2. Do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop and surface it.
3. Flip `(current)` -> `(done)`, before validation and the commit.
4. Validate the artifact (the medium-specific commands are in [custom.md](../custom.md)).
   Skip-able for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out.
5. Say "ready to commit" and stop. The user reviews the working-copy diff; iterate until
   complete.
6. Write the description: <=72-col conventional title, then a body whose intro names the
   problem this commit resolves and whose bullets record what changed, one per distinct change.
   No version in either, and no why/how (chores, todo, and the session hold those). See
   [Commit description](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commit-description).
7. Show title + body and stop for review. This review covers the push only when the user's go
   explicitly includes it.
8. On the user's go: `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`. Never pre-commit with
   `jj commit`; never hand-write `ochid:` trailers.

Reviewed. Four findings, worst first.

**1. The title length limit contradicts itself, four ways, and I made it worse today.** `cycle-protocol.md:273` says `<=50 chars total`. Three other places say 72: `cycle.md:63` ("<=72-col conventional title"), `prose.md:15` ("commit titles and bodies at <=72"), `prose.md:25` and `:140` ("the <=72-col title", "the <=72-col first line"). cycle-protocol is the declared authority on disagreement, so the binding limit is **50**, and three files misstate it. I rewrote both `cycle.md:63` and the `### Title` bullet in this step and left them disagreeing.

The intent is almost certainly the classic git convention: **50 for the subject, 72 for the body wrap.** `prose.md:15` conflates the two by naming one number for both. Recommended fix: 50 for the title everywhere, 72 for body wrap only. Workable here in practice, since this cycle's titles came out at 43 and 44 characters.

**2. The body content rule is now stated twice, nearly verbatim, in two files.** `prose.md:36-48` and `cycle-protocol.md:287-306` both carry intro-names-the-problem, one-bullet-per-distinct-change, files-sharing-a-gist-share-a-bullet, by-count-once-enumerating-stops-informing, and the why/how-lives-elsewhere sentence. That is the exact "detail written twice drifts" failure these files warn about, and `cycle-protocol.md:305` even ends by pointing at prose.md for "full bullet-content rules" while having just restated them. I created this duplication today by editing both to say the same thing.

Recommended: prose.md owns bullet content, since it already claims that job. cycle-protocol's `### Body` keeps only what is protocol-specific, the wrap plus the work-repo vs bot-repo split, and defers the rest.

**3. The example block at `cycle-protocol.md:294-300` is stale in two ways.** I changed its first line to `- path/to/file1: gist` but left `first distinct change` / `second distinct change` hanging under it, which re-implies the per-file model the rule just replaced. And "continuation indented 5" contradicts `prose.md:15`, which specifies two-space continuations. That second one is pre-existing and I edited around it.

**4. Gap: nothing bounds the body's length.** The intro is specified as one paragraph, but the bullet list has no guidance, which is odd for a change whose whole aim was shorter bodies. My drafted body runs 40 lines. Compliant by the letter, still long. A sentence would help: the record scales with distinct changes, and any bullet wanting a paragraph belongs in chores instead.

**And one honest note on the draft I just showed you:** `prose.md:37` says full sentences are discouraged in body bullets, and several of mine are full sentences ("the as-built rung is the one exception, and a version named as a specimen is distinguished from one used as an identifier"). The draft is mildly out of compliance with its own rule.

Findings 1 and 3 are outright defects and I would fix both. Finding 2 is a structural call on the authority file, so it is yours: consolidate now, or record it as a Todo and let the family convergence deal with it, since the same duplication may exist vc-x1-side. Whichever you pick, the description needs a redraft afterwards, and the fixes are small enough that I would rather not push a rule set that contradicts itself on the first line of every commit.

**What problem are we trying to solve?**

A step of a cycle had two names, its title and its version, and the record kept the fragile one. A rebase or a renumber changes a version; nothing changes a title. The 2026-08-01 renumber proved it: two published versions moved, and every transcript and pasted report naming them became unreadable, so `custom.md` had to grow a hand-written decoder table.

And yes, the title is the answer to that: `steps are titles, versions are stamps` says which of the two names a step keeps, and what the other one is demoted to.

**What did we do?**

- the title is a step's only name: no step number, and no version in a ladder rung, a chores header, a Done entry or a commit
- the title was made strong enough for the job: unambiguous within its cycle and within its chores file, where it is also an anchor
- one exception, the chores as-built rung, which records what a landed commit carried beside that commit's SHA; a fact about a commit rather than a name for a step, waiting for the same moment the SHA does, and it is the decoder the renumber needed
- backfilled the dynamic warmup ladder, eight rungs whose commits landed on `main` two cycles ago, so that decoder now exists where it was missing
- three consequences followed: Done entries became a bold title with sub-bullets once the version stopped being the eye's landmark, commit bodies became an intro plus what changed with the reasoning left to chores, and a topic bookmark is now a draft whose ladder is kept self-consistent until it lands

**As a body that is 25 lines, and the shape needs no new structure.** Your two questions map exactly onto Prose form's intro-plus-bullets. What was wrong was the instruction, not the shape: `prose.md:13` says the intro explains "the *why* or the high-level *what*", which is vague enough to produce either. The sharper version is **the intro states the problem, the bullets state what was done about it, and the title answers the problem.**

Two things that fell out of writing it this way, worth noticing before we set the rule:

- **The problem statement earns the date and the evidence.** "2026-08-01" and the decoder table belong here, not in chores, because without them the first bullet reads as taste. That contradicts what I wrote into the rules today, which pushed all reasoning to chores. The right line is narrower: the *problem* lives in the body, the *deliberation* lives in chores.
- **The trailing "Rationale ... in chores-06" line is now nearly redundant.** The body explains itself. The pointer is still worth one line, since the three passes and the accepted costs are genuinely elsewhere, but it stopped carrying the weight.

or the high-level *what*, then a `-` bullet list for the details. Wrap lines at <=100 cols,
commit titles at <=50 and commit bodies at <=72 (bullet continuations indent two spaces); existing text
re-wraps when touched, no mass sweeps. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs: they hide the structure
that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without naming their relationship is
the same failure at sentence scale; see [Semicolons inside bullets](#semicolons-inside-bullets)
and [Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).

Surfaces that use this shape:

- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files; see
  [Doc comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and bot-repo). The <=72-col title is the
  commit-specific add-on; see [Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow).
- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`; see
  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).

# Cycle checklists

Checklists for the moments where slips happen: committing, pushing, closing out. The full
protocol, with rationale and recovery procedures, is
[cycle-protocol.md](../notes/cycle-protocol.md); on any disagreement, that file wins. Re-read
the relevant checklist immediately before the action; don't run it from memory.

Universal file, shared with the template repository; a proposed change is edited here and
converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).

## The cycle at a glance

Every change runs as a **cycle**: an optional Preparation step -> Work steps -> a Close-out
step, one commit each. The ladder lists them in order and identifies each by its title, with no
number and no version; where the version-of-record lives and how often it is bumped are in
[versioning.md](../notes/versioning.md). Read
[cycle-protocol.md](../notes/cycle-protocol.md) before any commit work, and before any push,
cycle or not.

## Committing vs pushing

A cycle rung is committed *by* `vc-x1 push`; never pre-commit it with `jj commit`. Push's
commit stages commit both repos with the approved title/body and stamp each new commit's
`ochid:` trailer (see [ochid trailers](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)); a
pre-committed rung leaves `@` empty and push mints a stamped empty duplicate (bugs.md #6). In
an instruction, "commit", "push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push`. A bare `jj commit`
is asked for by name ("local commit", "just `jj commit`") and is only for work that never
publishes (local-only saves and loop-and-squash intermediates), with no `ochid:`. The approval
around a push, interactive by default and waived only by an explicit scoped delegation, is the
cycle protocol's [Pushing policy](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#policy).

## Topic bookmarks are drafts

A topic bookmark is a draft until it lands on a permanent branch; pushed there is not published.
So keep the series inside it self-consistent: inserting or reordering a step edits the ladder in
the rungs that already committed an older version of it, not only at the tip.

- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
  `jj describe`, so hard rule 4 stays intact and the `ochid:` trailers ride along untouched
  (they carry change ids, which survive a rewrite).
- **Then force-push the bookmark**, under the same approval as any other push.
- **Exceptions, where self-consistency is not worth its cost**: the bookmark has already landed;
  another branch is stacked on it, so the rewrite becomes someone else's rebase; or the ladder
  is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees.

The squash-form ladder below never meets this, since nothing on it is pushed. The rule is for the
multi-commit shape, whose rungs publish one at a time. Full statement in the protocol's
[Topic bookmarks are drafts](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts).

## Per-commit checklist

Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out), per the protocol's
[Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow):

1. Mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
2. Do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop and surface it.
3. Flip `(current)` -> `(done)`, before validation and the commit.
4. Validate the artifact (the medium-specific commands are in [custom.md](../custom.md)).
   Skip-able for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out.
5. Say "ready to commit" and stop. The user reviews the working-copy diff; iterate until
   complete.
6. Write the description: <=72-col conventional title, then a body whose intro names the
   problem this commit resolves and whose bullets record what changed, one per distinct change.
   No version in either, and no why/how (chores, todo, and the session hold those). See
   [Commit description](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commit-description).
7. Show title + body and stop for review. This review covers the push only when the user's go
   explicitly includes it.
8. On the user's go: `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`. Never pre-commit with
   `jj commit`; never hand-write `ochid:` trailers.

## Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist

Within a sub-cycle ladder, per the protocol's
[per-Work-commit contract](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder):

1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@`.
2. Do the commit's work.
3. Run the fast validation (named in [custom.md](../custom.md)). Non-negotiable.
4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: scratch working title. This first-time authoring is
   the one permitted describe; the commit is never published and never carries a trailer.

Nothing on a ladder is pushed; the close-out squash
(`jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .`) collapses it, and `vc-x1 push` then
publishes the single commit.

## Before any push

- This specific push has the user's explicit approval. Approval of a plan that includes a push
  is not push approval; "commit and push" names the destination, not a waiver of the reviews.
  Only an explicit scoped delegation ("do all of X, don't check in") waives the stops, for that
  bounded task only; destructive ops still pause.
- Validation ran, and passed, after the last edit.
- Closing words are already written; nothing follows the turn's final push (next checklist).

## After the final push: hard stop

Once the turn's final push or bot-repo squash-push is invoked, do no further work: no
verification, no summary, no next-step offers, no edits, until the user speaks. Put all closing
words *before* the invoke. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a visible token
after the tool returns; if so, emit a bare acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary
or more work. Post-push verification happens next turn at the user's direction. A standing
delegation makes intermediate pushes just steps; the hard stop lands on the turn's *final*
push. See
[After push or squash-push](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#after-push-or-squash-push-stop-and-wait).

## Close-out checklist

The cycle's last step, per the protocol's
[Close-out](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#close-out):

1. Move the picked-up item from `## In Progress` to a `## Done` entry: a bold title line with its
   chores `[N]` ref, detail as sub-bullets (see
   [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form)).
2. Finalize the chores section: sync the header to the final commit title (and every anchor
   back-reference), add design subsections; the intro and As-built rungs are already there.
3. Full validation, mandatory.
4. Update `notes/README.md` if functionality changed.
5. At push time, surface the shape options (squash / trapezoid / keep separate) and wait for
   the user's choice. The trapezoid recipe is
   [in the protocol](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe); its step 4 is
   `jj git push`, not `vc-x1 push`.
6. Backfill the chores as-built ladder refs (and any remaining legacy `Commits:` lines) for
   the commits the previous push made permanent; never record a SHA that is not on a permanent
   branch.

## vc-x1 push behaviors to keep in mind

Three, independent of project language:

- **No checks of the project's own.** vc-x1 assumes nothing about a repo's contents beyond
  `.jj` and `.vc-config.toml`, and runs no build or tests. The medium's validation is the
  per-commit flow's job, run *before* invoking `vc-x1 push`. The one check that remains is
  `push-work` verifying the bookmark's remote refs are tracked, which is its own precondition.
- **Rerunning is safe.** Push keeps no state and cannot resume. Every stage no-ops when its
  work is already done, so a failed run is re-run, not resumed. If a run fails, push stops and
  reports; getting the repos back to a sensible state is the user's call, not something the
  tool infers.
- **ochid trailers** are injected by `vc-x1 push` itself, so don't hand-write them into the
  commit body or `--title`/`--body`.

[Prose form](../agent-data/prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets), wrap <=72. The intro is one
paragraph naming the problem this commit resolves. Bullet content differs per repo:

- **Work-repo body**: one bullet per *distinct change* rather than per file, with sub-bullets for
  detail. Files sharing one gist share a bullet, named by common path or glob, and by count once
  enumerating stops informing:

  ```
  - path/to/file1: gist
    - first distinct change
    - second distinct change, wrapping to next line
       with continuation indented 5
  - agent-data/*.md: one gist covering several files
  ```

  This list is the source of truth for the cycle's mechanical change record, and it is nothing
  more than that: the *why* and *how* live in the chores section, the `## Todo` entry, and the
  session the `ochid:` trailer names, each reachable from the commit by construction. Full
  bullet-content rules are in
  [agent-data/prose.md](../agent-data/prose.md#prose-form).

- **Bot-repo (`.claude`) body**: bullets describe
  in-session activity rather than work-repo changes.

### The body took two passes too

The first pass kept the body an edit list. It said "one bullet per *distinct change*, not per
file", called itself "source of truth for the mechanical edit list", and carried sub-rules for
when files share a gist, when to name a glob, and when to switch to a count. That was already an
improvement on one-bullet-per-file, and it survived exactly one use: writing this commit's own
description produced thirteen bullets that restated `git show --stat` in worse English.

The second pass (wink) dropped the list. A body is a **problem statement** then a **solution
statement**, in broad terms, and the diff is left to be the mechanical record it already is.

- **The first pass contradicted itself**, which is visible in the text it replaced: the rule
  warned that "restating what `git show --stat` already prints is a second copy that can drift"
  and then required a per-change list, which is the same duplication at a coarser grain.
- **The glob and count sub-rules existed only to manage the list.** With no list they have no
  job, so the rule got shorter rather than more qualified.
- **The problem statement has to answer for what it takes away.** Writing this one surfaced the
  test now in the rule: the problem said the version supplied the ordering, so the solution owed
  the reader what supplies it now. A body that raises a question and leaves it is not concise, it
  is incomplete.
- **A knock-on correction**, found by the same review: `notes.md` justified chores carrying no
  edit list on the ground that the *commit body* was the mechanical record. That was never quite
  right and is now plainly wrong, and the file already had the better formulation a few lines
  later ("Git owns the mechanical record"). It is now a three-way split: the diff is mechanical,
  the body is problem and solution, chores is the design thinking.
- **Four contradictions were cleared in the same pass**, all of them ours and most of them
  introduced earlier the same day: the body rule stated in full in two files, `prose.md` still
  calling bodies "file-by-file" in one place while forbidding it in another, two examples teaching
  the abandoned shape, and the title length limit reading `<=50` in the authority file against
  `<=72` in three others. The 50 stands, and body wrap stays 72.

Two facts settle it:

- **`prose.md:62` already glosses it your way**: "**Problem statement** (the why)". So the file has treated a problem statement as a form of the why all along, and line 13 simply never said so.
- **There are no inbound links to `#problem--plan-shape`**, so that section can be retitled for free.

**Yes to your change, with one adjustment.** I would not list "or the problem" as a third equal option, because "or" lets a vague why claim compliance, while two surfaces *require* the problem form (`prose.md:37` for commit bodies, `cycle-protocol.md:113` for the picked-up item). Phrasing it as the sharpest form keeps that:

```
a short intro that explains the *why* or the high-level *what*, sharpened to a
*problem statement* where a surface calls for one, then a `-` bullet list for the details
```

**And there is a consolidation worth taking while we are here.** We now have two named pairs that are the same shape in different tenses:

- problem + **plan** (`## In Progress`, chores intros, `## Todo`): what *will* be done
- problem + **solution** (commit bodies): what *was* done

`### Problem + plan shape` currently lists three surfaces and omits commit bodies, so the body rule reads as a separate invention rather than the same shape past-tense. Folding commit bodies in as the fourth surface, with the second half chosen by tense, turns two concepts into one. That also means the section title stops fitting, and `### Problem-first shape` covers all four.

Net effect: one shape named once, four surfaces listed under it, and line 13 pointing at it. The commit-body bullet in "Bullet content differs by surface" then only has to say what is *specific* to commit bodies, which is the no-file-list rule and the broad-terms rule.

Want me to apply both, the line 13 rewording and the consolidation? It is two edits in one file, plus a line in the chores narrative recording that the two pairs turned out to be one shape.

# Cycle checklists

Checklists for the moments where slips happen: committing, pushing, closing out. The full
protocol, with rationale and recovery procedures, is
[cycle-protocol.md](../notes/cycle-protocol.md); on any disagreement, that file wins. Re-read
the relevant checklist immediately before the action; don't run it from memory.

Universal file, shared with the template repository; a proposed change is edited here and
converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).

## The cycle at a glance

Every change runs as a **cycle**: an optional Preparation step -> Work steps -> a Close-out
step, one commit each. The ladder lists them in order and identifies each by its title, with no
number and no version; where the version-of-record lives and how often it is bumped are in
[versioning.md](../notes/versioning.md). Read
[cycle-protocol.md](../notes/cycle-protocol.md) before any commit work, and before any push,
cycle or not.

## Committing vs pushing

A cycle rung is committed *by* `vc-x1 push`; never pre-commit it with `jj commit`. Push's
commit stages commit both repos with the approved title/body and stamp each new commit's
`ochid:` trailer (see [ochid trailers](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)); a
pre-committed rung leaves `@` empty and push mints a stamped empty duplicate (bugs.md #6). In
an instruction, "commit", "push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push`. A bare `jj commit`
is asked for by name ("local commit", "just `jj commit`") and is only for work that never
publishes (local-only saves and loop-and-squash intermediates), with no `ochid:`. The approval
around a push, interactive by default and waived only by an explicit scoped delegation, is the
cycle protocol's [Pushing policy](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#policy).

## Topic bookmarks are drafts

A topic bookmark is a draft until it lands on a permanent branch; pushed there is not published.
So keep the series inside it self-consistent: inserting or reordering a step edits the ladder in
the rungs that already committed an older version of it, not only at the tip.

- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
  `jj describe`, so hard rule 4 stays intact and the `ochid:` trailers ride along untouched
  (they carry change ids, which survive a rewrite).
- **Then force-push the bookmark**, under the same approval as any other push.
- **Exceptions, where self-consistency is not worth its cost**: the bookmark has already landed;
  another branch is stacked on it, so the rewrite becomes someone else's rebase; or the ladder
  is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees.

The squash-form ladder below never meets this, since nothing on it is pushed. The rule is for the
multi-commit shape, whose rungs publish one at a time. Full statement in the protocol's
[Topic bookmarks are drafts](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts).

## Per-commit checklist

Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out), per the protocol's
[Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow):

1. Mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
2. Do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop and surface it.
3. Flip `(current)` -> `(done)`, before validation and the commit.
4. Validate the artifact (the medium-specific commands are in [custom.md](../custom.md)).
   Skip-able for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out.
5. Say "ready to commit" and stop. The user reviews the working-copy diff; iterate until
   complete.
6. Write the description: a <=50-col conventional title, then a problem statement and a solution
   statement, both broad, wrapped at <=72. No version in either, no file list (the diff is the
   mechanical record), and no why/how (chores, todo, and the session hold those). See
   [Commit description](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commit-description).
7. Show title + body and stop for review. This review covers the push only when the user's go
   explicitly includes it.
8. On the user's go: `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`. Never pre-commit with
   `jj commit`; never hand-write `ochid:` trailers.

## Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist

Within a sub-cycle ladder, per the protocol's
[per-Work-commit contract](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder):

1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@`.
2. Do the commit's work.
3. Run the fast validation (named in [custom.md](../custom.md)). Non-negotiable.
4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: scratch working title. This first-time authoring is
   the one permitted describe; the commit is never published and never carries a trailer.

Nothing on a ladder is pushed; the close-out squash
(`jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .`) collapses it, and `vc-x1 push` then
publishes the single commit.

## Before any push

- This specific push has the user's explicit approval. Approval of a plan that includes a push
  is not push approval; "commit and push" names the destination, not a waiver of the reviews.
  Only an explicit scoped delegation ("do all of X, don't check in") waives the stops, for that
  bounded task only; destructive ops still pause.
- Validation ran, and passed, after the last edit.
- Closing words are already written; nothing follows the turn's final push (next checklist).

## After the final push: hard stop

Once the turn's final push or bot-repo squash-push is invoked, do no further work: no
verification, no summary, no next-step offers, no edits, until the user speaks. Put all closing
words *before* the invoke. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a visible token
after the tool returns; if so, emit a bare acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary
or more work. Post-push verification happens next turn at the user's direction. A standing
delegation makes intermediate pushes just steps; the hard stop lands on the turn's *final*
push. See
[After push or squash-push](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#after-push-or-squash-push-stop-and-wait).

## Close-out checklist

The cycle's last step, per the protocol's
[Close-out](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#close-out):

1. Move the picked-up item from `## In Progress` to a `## Done` entry: a bold title line with its
   chores `[N]` ref, detail as sub-bullets (see
   [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form)).
2. Finalize the chores section: sync the header to the final commit title (and every anchor
   back-reference), add design subsections; the intro and As-built rungs are already there.
3. Full validation, mandatory.
4. Update `notes/README.md` if functionality changed.
5. At push time, surface the shape options (squash / trapezoid / keep separate) and wait for
   the user's choice. The trapezoid recipe is
   [in the protocol](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe); its step 4 is
   `jj git push`, not `vc-x1 push`.
6. Backfill the chores as-built ladder refs (and any remaining legacy `Commits:` lines) for
   the commits the previous push made permanent; never record a SHA that is not on a permanent
   branch.

## vc-x1 push behaviors to keep in mind

Three, independent of project language:

- **No checks of the project's own.** vc-x1 assumes nothing about a repo's contents beyond
  `.jj` and `.vc-config.toml`, and runs no build or tests. The medium's validation is the
  per-commit flow's job, run *before* invoking `vc-x1 push`. The one check that remains is
  `push-work` verifying the bookmark's remote refs are tracked, which is its own precondition.
- **Rerunning is safe.** Push keeps no state and cannot resume. Every stage no-ops when its
  work is already done, so a failed run is re-run, not resumed. If a run fails, push stops and
  reports; getting the repos back to a sensible state is the user's call, not something the
  tool infers.
- **ochid trailers** are injected by `vc-x1 push` itself, so don't hand-write them into the
  commit body or `--title`/`--body`.

version, a concise stamp that also gave the steps their order. A step

- a Done entry is a bold title with sub-bullets, and a commit body is
  a problem statement plus a solution statement

  until it lands

Written 2026-08-05 by the session that built the pending step, for the fresh session that reviews
it. Scratch, gitignored, delete when the step lands. Acquaint first (`AGENTS.md`, `custom.md`,

  `## In Progress` block. Full validation is therefore mandatory and **passed**: `cargo fmt` clean,

  review. `tmp/title.txt` (43 chars) and `tmp/body.txt` (all lines <=72) hold the approved-pending-
  review description.

  dogfooded on a real cycle.

## What the step does

Takes both the version and the step number out of durable prose, so a step is identified by its
title alone. Its own record is chores-06 `## docs: steps are titles, versions are stamps`, with the
`## Done` entry and ref `[85]` in `TODO.md`. It also clears backfill debt: `## feat: dynamic warmup`
had eight rungs on literal `[[N]]` placeholders despite all eight commits being ancestors of `main`,

Errors and contradictions, not redesign. Useful checks:

- **The body against the diff.** Every claim in `tmp/body.txt` should be true of the working copy.
- **Contradictions across the agent-files.** The commit-body rule, the title length limit, and the
  as-built rung form were each edited more than once today. An earlier pass found six conflicts by
  grepping for `file-by-file`, `distinct change`, `mechanical`, `<=50`, `<=72`, `step-N`; that grep
  is worth re-running.

  `### Problem-first shape` and `### Step numbers are positional` to
  `### Steps are named, not numbered`; `cycle-protocol.md` `## Numbering` to `## Step naming`;
  `versioning.md` `## Step numbering` to `## Suffix scheme`. Inbound links were re-pointed and
  verified, but re-verify.
- **Width and punctuation.** <=100 in notes, <=72 in the body, no `—` `–` `…` `→` `≤` `×`.

Each of these was argued and decided with wink today. Reasoning is in chores-06.

- A step has a **title and no number**; ladder position comes from the list.
- A title must be unambiguous **within its cycle and within its chores file** (anchor collisions),
  and may repeat across history.
- **One prose surface records a version**, the chores as-built rung, beside that commit's SHA, and
  it takes the SHA's timing, so an unlanded rung carries neither.
- A commit body is a **problem statement then a solution statement**, broad, no file list.
- A **topic bookmark is a draft** until it lands on `main`.
- `## Done` entries are a **bold title with sub-bullets**.
- The manifest keeps its `X.Y.Z-N` suffix scheme. Making the suffix a step number, or a slugified
  title, were both considered and rejected.

- `tmp/body.txt` has **no "details in chores" pointer**. The rules say chores, todo and the session
  are reachable by construction via the ladder ref and the `ochid:` trailer, so a pointer restates
  it. Add it back if you disagree.

  have renumbered two design citations for cosmetics.

family. Our outbound mailbox (`../vc-x1-template/messages/vc-x1.md`) still shows only 2026-08-03.
The plan is to send after the dogfood, so the reply carries evidence rather than intent.

## Hard constraints

- **Never push without explicit approval for that push** (hard rule 2), and stop dead after the
  turn's final push (hard rule 3).
- The rung is committed by `vc-x1 push`, never pre-committed with `jj commit` (hard rule 1). Note
  `custom.md`: the installed binary predates the scope rename, so it takes `--scope=code|bot`.
- Read the checklist in `agent-data/cycle.md` immediately before acting, not from memory.

Rebase `measure-reproducibility` (three commits, an in-flight cycle) onto `agent-files-model`, then
work its steps, refining the rules as they get used. Expect conflicts in `TODO.md`,
`notes/chores/chores-06.md` and `custom.md`, since this step and 0.24.1 rewrote all three. No
`src/` conflicts. The `custom.md` conflict is the interesting one: it forces the reclassification
test on real content.
